Functions · lines and graphs

Gradient and the forms of a line

  • Gradient m=x2​−x1​y2​−y1​​m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁): the rate of change of yy per unit of xx.
  • Gradient-intercept form: y=mx+cy = mx + c, where cc is the yy-intercept.
  • Point-gradient form: y−y1​=m(x−x1​)y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) through the point (x1​,y1​)(x₁, y₁).
  • General form: ax+by+d=0ax + by + d = 0.
  • A road climbing 1.2 m over 15 m horizontally has gradient 151.2​=0.081.2/15 = 0.08, an 8% incline.
Worked example Functions · lines and graphs

The line through two points

Question
Find the equation of the line through A(2,5)A(2, 5) and B(6,−3)B(6, −3). Give your answer in the form ax+by+d=0ax + by + d = 0, where aa, bb, d∈Zd ∈ ℤ.
  1. 1
    Gradient: m=6−2−3−5​=4−8​=−2m = (−3 − 5)/(6 − 2) = (−8)/4 = −2
  2. 2
    Point-gradient form through AA: y−5=−2(x−2)y − 5 = −2(x − 2)
  3. 3
    Expand: y=−2x+9y = −2x + 9
  4. 4
    Move every term to one side: 2x+y−9=02x + y − 9 = 0
Answer
2x+y−9=02x + y − 9 = 0
⚠️ Watch out
subtract the coordinates in the same order. 6−25−(−3)​=2(5 − (−3))/(6 − 2) = 2 has the wrong sign.
Functions · lines and graphs

Parallel and perpendicular lines

  • Parallel lines have equal gradients: m1​=m2​m₁ = m₂.
  • Perpendicular lines: m1​×m2​=−1m₁ × m₂ = −1, so m2​=−m1​1​m₂ = −1/m₁ (the negative reciprocal).
  • To read a gradient from general form, rearrange to y=mx+cy = mx + c. For 2x+5y−7=02x + 5y − 7 = 0: y=−52​x+57​y = −2/5x + 7/5, so m=−52​m = −2/5.
  • Any line perpendicular to it has gradient 25​5/2.
Calculate
?The line LL passes through (3,1)(3, 1) and is perpendicular to 2x+5y−7=02x + 5y − 7 = 0. Find the yy-intercept of LL. Give your answer as a decimal.
Functions · lines and graphs

Functions, domain, range and inverses

  • A function gives each input exactly one output. Notation: f(x)f(x), v(t)v(t), C(n)C(n).
  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs. f(x)=2−x​f(x) = √(2 − x) has domain x≤2x ≤ 2 and range f(x)≥0f(x) ≥ 0.
  • The inverse function f−1f⁻¹ undoes ff: solving f(x)=10f(x) = 10 is the same as finding f−1(10)f⁻¹(10).
  • The graph of f−1f⁻¹ is the reflection of ff in y=xy = x. Only one-to-one functions have inverses; the domain of f−1f⁻¹ is the range of ff.
Quick check
?The function ff is defined by f(x)=x−3​+1f(x) = √(x − 3) + 1, for x≥3x ≥ 3. Which is the range of ff?
Functions · lines and graphs

Key features of graphs, with technology

  • Sketch: the shape, with axes and key features labelled. Draw: accurate, to scale.
  • Key features: intercepts, zeros (roots of f(x)=0f(x) = 0), maximum and minimum points, vertex, symmetry, vertical and horizontal asymptotes.
  • To solve f(x)=g(x)f(x) = g(x), graph both on your GDC and find the intersection points. A GDC also graphs sums and differences such as y=f(x)−g(x)y = f(x) − g(x), whose zeros are the same xx-values.
  • On a no-calculator paper, set f(x)=g(x)f(x) = g(x) and solve algebraically instead.

Where two graphs meet

Question
f(x)=x2−3xf(x) = x² − 3x and g(x)=2x−3g(x) = 2x − 3. Find the xx-coordinates of the points where the graphs of ff and gg intersect. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
  1. 1
    Set the functions equal: x2−3x=2x−3x² − 3x = 2x − 3
  2. 2
    Rearrange to zero: x2−5x+3=0x² − 5x + 3 = 0
  3. 3
    Use the intersect tool on your GDC (or the quadratic formula): x=25±13​​x = (5 ± √13)/2
Answer
x=0.697x = 0.697 or x=4.30x = 4.30
⚠️ Watch out
a GDC finds one intersection at a time. Check the window shows every crossing so you do not miss one.
Calculate

seconds
Mission check

?Taxi A charges £3.50 plus £1.20 per km. Taxi B charges £6.00 plus £0.95 per km. When does the cheaper one switch?

Each cost is a linear function of distance: the fixed fee is the yy-intercept and the price per km is the gradient. The cheaper taxi switches where the lines intersect: 3.50+1.20d=6.00+0.95d3.50 + 1.20d = 6.00 + 0.95d gives d=10d = 10 km, where both cost £15.50. Below 10 km A's lower fee wins; beyond it B's smaller gradient wins.

Functions · composites, inverses and transformations

Composite functions

  • (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))(f ° g)(x) = f(g(x)): apply gg first, then ff to the result.
  • With f(x)=2x+3f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x)=x2g(x) = x²: (f∘g)(x)=2x2+3(f ° g)(x) = 2x² + 3 but (g∘f)(x)=(2x+3)2(g ° f)(x) = (2x + 3)². Order matters.
  • In context: n(t)=50tn(t) = 50t phones are made in tt hours and C(n)=200+4nC(n) = 200 + 4n is their cost in £. Then (C∘n)(t)=200+200t(C ° n)(t) = 200 + 200t is the cost after tt hours.
  • g(x)g(x) must lie in the domain of ff for f(g(x))f(g(x)) to exist.
Calculate
?f(x)=3x−1f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x)=x2+2g(x) = x² + 2. Find (g∘f)(2)(g ° f)(2).
Functions · composites, inverses and transformations

Inverse functions

  • f−1f⁻¹ undoes ff: (f∘f−1)(x)=(f−1∘f)(x)=x(f ° f⁻¹)(x) = (f⁻¹ ° f)(x) = x, the identity function.
  • To undo a chain of steps, undo the last step first, like taking off shoes before socks.
  • Method: write y=f(x)y = f(x), rearrange to make xx the subject, then swap xx and yy.
  • An inverse exists only if ff is one-to-one. If it is not, restrict the domain. The domain of f−1f⁻¹ is the range of ff.
Worked example Functions · composites, inverses and transformations

An inverse with a restricted domain

Question
f(x)=(x−3)2−2f(x) = (x − 3)² − 2, for x≥3x ≥ 3. Find f−1(x)f⁻¹(x) and state its domain.
  1. 1
    Write y=(x−3)2−2y = (x − 3)² − 2 and add 2: y+2=(x−3)2y + 2 = (x − 3)²
  2. 2
    Square-root, taking the positive root because x≥3x ≥ 3: x−3=y+2​x − 3 = √(y + 2)
  3. 3
    Make xx the subject: x=3+y+2​x = 3 + √(y + 2)
  4. 4
    Swap xx and yy: f−1(x)=3+x+2​f⁻¹(x) = 3 + √(x + 2)
  5. 5
    The range of ff is f(x)≥−2f(x) ≥ −2, so the domain of f−1f⁻¹ is x≥−2x ≥ −2
Answer
f−1(x)=3+x+2​f⁻¹(x) = 3 + √(x + 2), x≥−2x ≥ −2
⚠️ Watch out
without the restriction x≥3x ≥ 3, ff is many-to-one (f(1)=f(5)=2f(1) = f(5) = 2) and has no inverse.
Quick check
?f(x)=3x+4​f(x) = (x + 4)/3. Which is f−1(x)f⁻¹(x)?
Functions · composites, inverses and transformations

Transformations of graphs

  • Translations: y=f(x)+by = f(x) + b moves the graph up bb; y=f(x−a)y = f(x − a) moves it right aa.
  • Reflections: y=−f(x)y = −f(x) in the xx-axis; y=f(−x)y = f(−x) in the yy-axis.
  • Stretches: y=pf(x)y = pf(x) is vertical, scale factor pp; y=f(qx)y = f(qx) is horizontal, scale factor q1​1/q.
  • Changes outside ff act on yy-values; changes inside act on xx-values, the opposite way to how they look.
Worked example Functions · composites, inverses and transformations

Order in a composite transformation

Question
Describe a sequence of transformations that maps y=x2y = x² onto y=3x2+2y = 3x² + 2.
  1. 1
    Multiply the outputs by 3: vertical stretch, scale factor 3, gives y=3x2y = 3x²
  2. 2
    Add 2 to the outputs: translation 2 units up (y=f(x)+2y = f(x) + 2 with b=2b = 2), gives y=3x2+2y = 3x² + 2
  3. 3
    Track a point: (1,1)→(1,3)→(1,5)(1, 1) → (1, 3) → (1, 5)
Answer
a vertical stretch with scale factor 3, followed by a translation of 2 units up
⚠️ Watch out
in the other order, y=x2+2y = x² + 2 stretched by 3 gives y=3x2+6y = 3x² + 6. The order matters.
Calculate
?The point P(6,−4)P(6, −4) lies on the graph of y=f(x)y = f(x). The graph is transformed to y=−2f(x)+5y = −2f(x) + 5. Find the yy-coordinate of the image of PP.
Sort it

Mission check

?f(x)=2x+3f(x) = 2x + 3 doubles, then adds 3. Why does f−1f⁻¹ subtract 3 first?

ff is a composite of two steps: double, then add 3. An inverse undoes them in reverse order, like taking off shoes before socks: subtract 3, then halve. So f−1(x)=2x−3​f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2, and f−1(13)=5f⁻¹(13) = 5.

Functions · quadratics

Three forms of a quadratic

  • A quadratic graph is a parabola: a>0a > 0 opens upwards (minimum), a<0a < 0 downwards (maximum).
  • Standard form f(x)=ax2+bx+cf(x) = ax² + bx + c: yy-intercept (0,c)(0, c); axis of symmetry x=−2ab​x = −b/2a.
  • Intercept form f(x)=a(x−p)(x−q)f(x) = a(x − p)(x − q): xx-intercepts (p,0)(p, 0) and (q,0)(q, 0); axis halfway, x=2p+q​x = (p + q)/2.
  • Vertex form f(x)=a(x−h)2+kf(x) = a(x − h)² + k: vertex (h,k)(h, k); axis x=hx = h.
  • x2−6x+5=(x−1)(x−5)=(x−3)2−4x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 1)(x − 5) = (x − 3)² − 4: one graph, three views.
Worked example Functions · quadratics

Changing between forms

Question
f(x)=2x2+8x−10f(x) = 2x² + 8x − 10. Write f(x)f(x) in the form a(x−h)2+ka(x − h)² + k and in the form a(x−p)(x−q)a(x − p)(x − q). Hence state the vertex and the xx-intercepts.
  1. 1
    Take out the factor 2 from the xx terms: 2(x2+4x)−102(x² + 4x) − 10
  2. 2
    Complete the square inside: 2[(x+2)2−4]−102[(x + 2)² − 4] − 10
  3. 3
    Multiply out the bracket and tidy: 2(x+2)2−8−10=2(x+2)2−182(x + 2)² − 8 − 10 = 2(x + 2)² − 18
  4. 4
    Factorise the standard form: 2(x2+4x−5)=2(x−1)(x+5)2(x² + 4x − 5) = 2(x − 1)(x + 5)
Answer
f(x)=2(x+2)2−18=2(x−1)(x+5)f(x) = 2(x + 2)² − 18 = 2(x − 1)(x + 5); vertex (−2,−18)(−2, −18); xx-intercepts (1,0)(1, 0) and (−5,0)(−5, 0)
⚠️ Watch out
the −4−4 inside the square bracket is also multiplied by 2. Writing 2(x+2)2−4−102(x + 2)² − 4 − 10 gives the wrong vertex (−2,−14)(−2, −14).

Functions · quadratics

Solving, and the discriminant

  • Solve ax2+bx+c=0ax² + bx + c = 0 by factorising, completing the square or the quadratic formula:
x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a
  • The solutions are the roots, or zeros of ff. Check them with your GDC where allowed.
  • The discriminant Δ=b2−4acΔ = b² − 4ac: Δ>0Δ > 0 two distinct real roots; Δ=0Δ = 0 two equal real roots (the graph touches the xx-axis); Δ<0Δ < 0 no real roots.

A quadratic inequality

Question
Solve 2x2+x−6≤02x² + x − 6 ≤ 0.
  1. 1
    Solve the equation first: 2x2+x−6=(2x−3)(x+2)=02x² + x − 6 = (2x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, so x=1.5x = 1.5 or x=−2x = −2
  2. 2
    Sketch: a=2>0a = 2 > 0, so the parabola opens upwards and is below the xx-axis between its zeros
  3. 3
    Include the endpoints, since the inequality is ≤≤
Answer
−2≤x≤1.5−2 ≤ x ≤ 1.5
⚠️ Watch out
for >0> 0 or ≥0≥ 0 with a>0a > 0, the solution is the two outside parts, x<px < p or x>qx > q, not one interval.

Mission check

?The jet follows h=−0.5x2+2x+0.5h = −0.5x² + 2x + 0.5, starting 0.5 m above the water. How far from the nozzle does it land in the water?

The jet lands where h=0h = 0. In vertex form h=−0.5(x−2)2+2.5h = −0.5(x − 2)² + 2.5, so the axis of symmetry is x=2x = 2; but the jet starts 0.5 m above the water, so symmetry only brings it back to nozzle height at 4 m. The quadratic formula gives x=2+5​≈4.24x = 2 + √5 ≈ 4.24 m, so the bowl must reach at least that far.

Functions · rational, exponential and log functions

Reciprocal and rational functions

  • The reciprocal function f(x)=x1​f(x) = 1/x, x=0x ≠ 0, has asymptotes x=0x = 0 and y=0y = 0.
  • It is self-inverse: f−1(x)=x1​f⁻¹(x) = 1/x, so its graph is symmetric in y=xy = x.
  • For f(x)=cx+dax+b​f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d): vertical asymptote x=−cd​x = −d/c (denominator zero); horizontal asymptote y=ca​y = a/c (value as xx grows large).
  • A sketch shows every asymptote, as a dashed line, and both axis intercepts.
Worked example Functions · rational, exponential and log functions

Asymptotes and intercepts

Question
Sketch f(x)=x+32x−1​f(x) = (2x − 1)/(x + 3), stating its asymptotes and axis intercepts.
  1. 1
    Vertical asymptote, where the denominator is zero: x+3=0x + 3 = 0, so x=−3x = −3
  2. 2
    Horizontal asymptote, y=ca​y = a/c: y=12​=2y = 2/1 = 2
  3. 3
    xx-intercept, where the numerator is zero: 2x−1=02x − 1 = 0, so (0.5,0)(0.5, 0)
  4. 4
    yy-intercept, f(0)=3−1​f(0) = (−1)/3: (0,−31​)(0, −1/3)
Answer
asymptotes x=−3x = −3 and y=2y = 2; intercepts (0.5,0)(0.5, 0) and (0,−31​)(0, −1/3)
⚠️ Watch out
the vertical asymptote is x=−cd​x = −d/c; reading x=3x = 3 from "x+3x + 3" is a sign slip.

Functions · rational, exponential and log functions

Exponential and logarithmic functions

  • Exponential: f(x)=axf(x) = a^x (a>0a > 0) and f(x)=exf(x) = e^x pass through (0,1)(0, 1), have range f(x)>0f(x) > 0 and horizontal asymptote y=0y = 0.
  • Logarithmic: f(x)=loga​xf(x) = log_a x and f(x)=lnxf(x) = ln x, domain x>0x > 0, pass through (1,0)(1, 0) and have vertical asymptote x=0x = 0.
  • They are inverses: loga​ax=xlog_a a^x = x and aloga​x=xa^(log_a x) = x, so their graphs are reflections in y=xy = x.
  • Any base can be changed to e: ax=exlnaa^x = e^(x ln a).
  • Exponential decay e−kxe^(−kx) (k>0k > 0): each increase of 1 in xx multiplies the value by the same factor e−ke^(−k), between 0 and 1.
Calculate
?Write 5x5^x in the form ekxe^kx. Find kk, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
Functions · rational, exponential and log functions

Solving equations analytically and graphically

  • To bring down a power, take logs: ax=ba^x = b gives x=loga​b=lnalnb​x = log_a b = (ln b)/(ln a).
  • Spot hidden quadratics: e2x=(ex)2e^2x = (e^x)², so substitute u=exu = e^x.
  • When there is no analytic method, as in ex=sinxe^x = sin x or x4+5x−7=0x⁴ + 5x − 7 = 0, use your GDC: graph both sides and find the intersections, or graph one side minus the other and find the zeros.
Worked example Functions · rational, exponential and log functions

A hidden quadratic

Question
Solve e2x−5ex+4=0e^2x − 5e^x + 4 = 0, giving exact answers.
  1. 1
    Substitute u=exu = e^x: u2−5u+4=0u² − 5u + 4 = 0
  2. 2
    Factorise: (u−1)(u−4)=0(u − 1)(u − 4) = 0, so u=1u = 1 or u=4u = 4
  3. 3
    Return to xx: ex=1e^x = 1 gives x=0x = 0; ex=4e^x = 4 gives x=ln4x = ln 4
Answer
x=0x = 0 or x=ln4x = ln 4
⚠️ Watch out
ex>0e^x > 0 for every xx, so a negative value of uu would give no solution and must be rejected.
Calculate

minutes

Mission check

?A model gives C(t)=20e−0.3tC(t) = 20e^(−0.3t) mg per litre. Why does the model's concentration never reach zero?

In the model, each hour multiplies the concentration by the same positive factor e−0.3≈0.741e^(−0.3) ≈ 0.741, so it loses a fixed fraction, not a fixed amount. Since e−0.3t>0e^(−0.3t) > 0 for every tt, the graph gets ever closer to the horizontal asymptote C=0C = 0 but never reaches it. In reality the drug soon falls below a level anyone can measure.

Functions · polynomials

Polynomial graphs, zeros and factors

  • A degree nn polynomial has at most nn real zeros: the xx-intercepts of y=P(x)y = P(x), the real roots of P(x)=0P(x) = 0.
  • Each root αα gives a factor (x−α)(x − α). Counting complex and repeated roots, there are exactly nn.
  • Single root: the graph crosses the axis. Double root: it touches and turns. Triple root: it crosses, flattening.
  • The sign of an​aₙ and the parity of nn fix the ends: y=x4−3x3−…y = x⁴ − 3x³ − … rises at both ends.
Sort it
?At each given root, does the graph cross or touch the xx-axis?

Functions · polynomials

The remainder and factor theorems

  • Remainder theorem: when P(x)P(x) is divided by (x−a)(x − a), the remainder is P(a)P(a).
  • Dividing by (ax−b)(ax − b), the remainder is P(ab​)P(b/a): use the value of xx that makes the divisor zero.
  • Factor theorem: (x−a)(x − a) is a factor of P(x)P(x) if and only if P(a)=0P(a) = 0.
  • To find unknown coefficients, turn each piece of information into an equation in them, then solve simultaneously.
Worked example Functions · polynomials

Finding unknown coefficients

Question
P(x)=x3+ax2+bx−6P(x) = x³ + ax² + bx − 6. (x−2)(x − 2) is a factor of P(x)P(x), and the remainder when P(x)P(x) is divided by (x+1)(x + 1) is −12−12. Find aa and bb.
  1. 1
    Factor theorem, P(2)=0P(2) = 0: 8+4a+2b−6=08 + 4a + 2b − 6 = 0, so 2a+b=−12a + b = −1
  2. 2
    Remainder theorem, P(−1)=−12P(−1) = −12: −1+a−b−6=−12−1 + a − b − 6 = −12, so a−b=−5a − b = −5
  3. 3
    Add the two equations: 3a=−63a = −6, so a=−2a = −2, then b=3b = 3
  4. 4
    Check: P(x)=x3−2x2+3x−6=(x−2)(x2+3)P(x) = x³ − 2x² + 3x − 6 = (x − 2)(x² + 3)
Answer
a=−2a = −2, b=3b = 3
⚠️ Watch out
dividing by (x+1)(x + 1) means substituting x=−1x = −1, not x=1x = 1.
Calculate

Worked example Functions · polynomials

Factorising a cubic fully

Question
Factorise P(x)=2x3+3x2−11x−6P(x) = 2x³ + 3x² − 11x − 6 fully and solve P(x)=0P(x) = 0.
  1. 1
    Try small factors of the constant term: P(1)=−12P(1) = −12, but P(2)=16+12−22−6=0P(2) = 16 + 12 − 22 − 6 = 0, so (x−2)(x − 2) is a factor
  2. 2
    Divide (or compare coefficients): P(x)=(x−2)(2x2+7x+3)P(x) = (x − 2)(2x² + 7x + 3)
  3. 3
    Factorise the quadratic: 2x2+7x+3=(2x+1)(x+3)2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3)
  4. 4
    Set each factor to zero: x=2x = 2, x=−21​x = −1/2, x=−3x = −3
Answer
P(x)=(x−2)(2x+1)(x+3)P(x) = (x − 2)(2x + 1)(x + 3); roots −3−3, −21​−1/2, 2
⚠️ Watch out
with a leading coefficient of 2, a root can be a fraction such as −21​−1/2: keep the factor as (2x+1)(2x + 1).
Functions · polynomials

Sum and product of the roots

For an​xn+an−1​xn−1+⋯+a1​x+a0​=0aₙ xⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁ x + a₀ = 0 with roots α1​,…,αn​α₁, …, αₙ: sum=an​−an−1​​product=an​(−1)na0​​sum = (−aₙ₋₁)/aₙ product = ((−1)ⁿ a₀)/aₙ

  • Why: an​(x−α1​)⋯(x−αn​)aₙ(x − α₁)⋯(x − αₙ) expands to an​xn−an​(α1​+⋯+αn​)xn−1+⋯+an​(−1)nα1​⋯αn​aₙ xⁿ − aₙ(α₁ + … + αₙ)xⁿ⁻¹ + … + aₙ(−1)ⁿα₁⋯αₙ.
  • Count every root: repeated roots as often as they occur, and complex roots too. x3−2x2+3x−6=0x³ − 2x² + 3x − 6 = 0 has roots 2 and ±3​i±√3 i: sum 2, product 6.
  • The formula is in the formula booklet; the sign (−1)n(−1)ⁿ is where marks are lost.

Mission check

?How can you add a quartic's four roots without finding any of them? Take 2x4−14x3+18x2+14x−20=02x⁴ − 14x³ + 18x² + 14x − 20 = 0.

Expanding an​(x−α)(x−β)(x−γ)(x−δ)aₙ(x − α)(x − β)(x − γ)(x − δ) puts −an​(α+β+γ+δ)−aₙ(α + β + γ + δ) in front of x3x³. So for 2x4−14x3+18x2+14x−20=02x⁴ − 14x³ + 18x² + 14x − 20 = 0 the four roots add to 2−(−14)​=7(−(−14))/2 = 7, without solving anything.

Mission 6

A function is its own inverse. What must its graph look like?

Make a guess: A function is its own inverse. What must its graph look like?

Functions · rational functions and transformations

Rational functions and their asymptotes

  • Vertical asymptotes: where the denominator is zero (and the numerator is not).
  • cx2+dx+eax+b​(ax + b)/(cx² + dx + e): the denominator's degree is higher, so y→0y → 0: horizontal asymptote y=0y = 0. Up to two vertical asymptotes.
  • dx+eax2+bx+c​(ax² + bx + c)/(dx + e): divide to get mx+k+dx+er​mx + k + r/(dx + e). The last term →0→ 0, so y=mx+ky = mx + k is an oblique asymptote.
  • A full sketch shows every asymptote (with its equation) and every axis intercept.
Worked example Functions · rational functions and transformations

Finding an oblique asymptote

Question
f(x)=x−22x2−x−3​f(x) = (2x² − x − 3)/(x − 2). Find the asymptotes and the axis intercepts of the graph of ff.
  1. 1
    Vertical asymptote where x−2=0x − 2 = 0: x=2x = 2
  2. 2
    Divide: 2x2−x−3=(x−2)(2x+3)+32x² − x − 3 = (x − 2)(2x + 3) + 3, so f(x)=2x+3+x−23​f(x) = 2x + 3 + 3/(x − 2)
  3. 3
    As x→±∞x → ±∞, x−23​→03/(x − 2) → 0: oblique asymptote y=2x+3y = 2x + 3
  4. 4
    Intercepts: (2x−3)(x+1)=0(2x − 3)(x + 1) = 0 gives x=23​x = 3/2 and x=−1x = −1; f(0)=−2−3​=23​f(0) = (−3)/(−2) = 3/2
Answer
x=2x = 2 and y=2x+3y = 2x + 3; intercepts (−1,0)(−1, 0), (23​,0)(3/2, 0), (0,23​)(0, 3/2)
⚠️ Watch out
the remainder is not part of the asymptote. y=2x+3y = 2x + 3 is the quotient only.
Quick check

Functions · rational functions and transformations

Odd, even and self-inverse functions

  • Even: f(−x)=f(x)f(−x) = f(x). The graph is symmetric in the yy-axis: x2x², cosxcos x.
  • Odd: f(−x)=−f(x)f(−x) = −f(x). Rotational symmetry of order 2 about the origin: x3x³, sinxsin x, tanxtan x.
  • f−1f⁻¹ exists only where ff is one-to-one, so you may need to restrict the domain: x2x² with x≥0x ≥ 0 has inverse x​√x. The graph of f−1f⁻¹ is the reflection of ff in y=xy = x.
  • Self-inverse: f−1(x)=f(x)f⁻¹(x) = f(x), so f(f(x))=xf(f(x)) = x. Examples: x1​1/x, 5−x5 − x, x−22x+1​(2x + 1)/(x − 2).
Calculate
?The function f(x)=x−k3x+5​f(x) = (3x + 5)/(x − k), x=kx ≠ k, is self-inverse. Find the value of the constant kk.
Sort it

Worked example Functions · rational functions and transformations

Solving g(x)≥f(x)g(x) ≥ f(x): a rational inequality

Question
Solve x−2x+1​≥2(x + 1)/(x − 2) ≥ 2.
  1. 1
    Don't multiply by x−2x − 2 (it may be negative). Subtract 2 and combine: x−2x+1−2(x−2)​=x−25−x​≥0(x + 1 − 2(x − 2))/(x − 2) = (5 − x)/(x − 2) ≥ 0
  2. 2
    Critical values, where the top or the bottom is zero: x=5x = 5 and x=2x = 2
  3. 3
    Sign table (the same method works for a factorised cubic ≥0≥ 0): negative for x<2x < 2, positive for 2<x<52 < x < 5, negative for x>5x > 5
  4. 4
    Include x=5x = 5 (the fraction is 0), exclude x=2x = 2 (undefined)
  5. 5
    Check with your GDC: y=x−2x+1​y = (x + 1)/(x − 2) is on or above y=2y = 2 only for 2<x≤52 < x ≤ 5
Answer
2<x≤52 < x ≤ 5
⚠️ Watch out
multiplying both sides by x−2x − 2 gives x≤5x ≤ 5 alone, which wrongly includes values below 2, where x−2x − 2 is negative.

Modulus and other transformations

GraphHow to get it from y=f(x)y = f(x)
y=∣f(x)∣y = | f(x) |reflect the parts below the xx-axis in the xx-axis
y=f(∣x∣)y = f(| x |)keep the part for x≥0x ≥ 0; reflect it in the yy-axis

  • Modulus equations: ∣f(x)∣=c|f(x)| = c means f(x)=cf(x) = c or f(x)=−cf(x) = −c.
  • Modulus inequalities: ∣f(x)∣<c|f(x)| < c means −c<f(x)<c−c < f(x) < c; use a graph or GDC when it gets harder.
Calculate
?How many integers xx satisfy ∣x2−4∣<3|x² − 4| < 3?
Mission check

?A function is its own inverse. What must its graph look like?

Reflecting a graph in y=xy = x always gives the graph of the inverse. For a self-inverse function that reflection must give back the same graph, so the graph is symmetric in the line y=xy = x, like y=x1​y = 1/x or y=x−22x+1​y = (2x + 1)/(x − 2).

Recap

Big ideas

  • A line has gradient m=x2​−x1​y2​−y1​​m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and can be written y=mx+cy = mx + c, y−y1​=m(x−x1​)y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) or ax+by+d=0ax + by + d = 0; parallel means m1​=m2​m₁ = m₂, perpendicular means m1​m2​=−1m₁ m₂ = −1.
  • A function has a domain (inputs) and a range (outputs); f−1f⁻¹ undoes ff, exists for one-to-one functions and is the reflection of ff in y=xy = x.
  • Key features (intercepts, zeros, maximum and minimum, asymptotes) and intersections come from a GDC or from solving f(x)=g(x)f(x) = g(x).
  • (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))(f ° g)(x) = f(g(x)): apply gg first; in general f∘g=g∘ff ° g ≠ g ° f.
  • f−1f⁻¹ undoes ff (last step first); it needs ff to be one-to-one, possibly after restricting the domain, and the domain of f−1f⁻¹ is the range of ff.
  • f(x)+bf(x) + b, −f(x)−f(x), pf(x)pf(x) act on yy-values; f(x−a)f(x − a), f(−x)f(−x), f(qx)f(qx) act on xx-values; the order of transformations matters.
  • Standard form gives the yy-intercept, intercept form the xx-intercepts, vertex form the vertex (h,k)(h, k); the axis of symmetry is x=−2ab​x = −b/2a.
  • Solve by factorising, completing the square or x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a; Δ=b2−4acΔ = b² − 4ac decides two, one repeated or no real roots.
  • For a quadratic inequality, find the roots, sketch the parabola and read off where it is above or below the axis.
  • f(x)=cx+dax+b​f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d) has vertical asymptote x=−cd​x = −d/c and horizontal asymptote y=ca​y = a/c; x1​1/x is its own inverse.
  • axa^x and loga​xlog_a x are inverse functions: ax>0a^x > 0 with asymptote y=0y = 0; loga​xlog_a x needs x>0x > 0 and has asymptote x=0x = 0; ax=exlnaa^x = e^(x ln a).
  • Solve with logs or a substitution such as u=exu = e^x when you can; otherwise find intersections or zeros on your GDC.
  • A root αα of P(x)=0P(x) = 0 means a factor (x−α)(x − α) and an xx-intercept; single roots cross, double roots touch.
  • Remainder on dividing by (ax−b)(ax − b) is P(ab​)P(b/a); (x−a)(x − a) is a factor exactly when P(a)=0P(a) = 0.
  • Sum of roots an​−an−1​​(−aₙ₋₁)/aₙ, product an​(−1)na0​​((−1)ⁿ a₀)/aₙ, counting complex and repeated roots.
  • Rational graphs: vertical asymptotes from the denominator; divide to find an oblique asymptote; mark all intercepts.
  • Even: f(−x)=f(x)f(−x) = f(x); odd: f(−x)=−f(x)f(−x) = −f(x); self-inverse: f(f(x))=xf(f(x)) = x, symmetric in y=xy = x.
  • Inequalities: one side zero, critical values, sign table; never multiply by something that could be negative. ∣f(x)∣<c|f(x)| < c means −c<f(x)<c−c < f(x) < c.
